{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=algorithmic+mechanisms+accountability+autonomous+systems+consequence+tracking+decision+trees&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.62311/nesx/rb-69ag-978-81-68314-31-3\", \"title\": [\"Computational Law and Responsible AI Governance for Algorithmic Accountability, Digital Rights and Autonomous Decision Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Abstract\\nComputational law can help translate selected norms and institutional duties into reviewable decision processes, while autonomous AI systems raise new questions about authority, evidence and remedy. This monograph develops a research framework for algorithmic accountability, digital rights and responsible governance using only relevant works in the supplied reference corpus. Ten themes cover machine-readable norms, effective remedies, lifecycle responsibility, causal impact assessment, explanation, model drift, generative provenance, policy-as-code, auditability and sectoral assurance. Five chapters progress from legal and institutional foundations to distributional evaluation, model and agent assurance, reproducible operations and applied governance. The central object is a consequential decision whose governing rule, evidence, model state, human intervention and avenue of challenge can be reconstructed. Proposed outputs include norm-to-code matrices, impact taxonomies, dated rollout panels, reason-giving tests, bounded agent manifests, policy registers and disputed-case audit packets. The framework distinguishes technical validation from legal authorization and preserves local interpretation across jurisdictions. It assesses whether a person can receive notice, correct evidence, contest an outcome and obtain a meaningful remedy under ordinary operating conditions. Public services, financial scoring and autonomous mobility provide contrasting research settings; no proposed experiment is described as an observed result. Independent review, counterexamples, incident recovery and longitudinal appeal evidence anchor the account of trustworthy deployment. The resulting evidence standard links computational methods to institutional duties without treating code as self-authorizing law.\\nKeywords\\ncomputational law, responsible AI, algorithmic accountability, digital rights, autonomous systems, policy-as-code, legal interpretation, procedural fairness, causal impact, distributional evaluation, contestability, meaningful remedy, reason-giving, model governance, agent permissions, formal assurance, generative AI, data lineage, audit evidence, human oversight, incident response</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.62311/nesx/rb-69ag-978-81-68314-31-3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 8, 30]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7485400\", \"title\": [\"Governing Algorithmic Decision-making: A Socio-technical Governance Framework for Enforcing Accountability in Autonomous Digital Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems into core organizational decision-making workflows has outpaced traditional governance structures. While these systems improve computational efficiency, they simultaneously obscure decision logic and subvert human oversight, creating a systemic \\\"governance gap\\\". Drawing upon Socio-Technical Systems (STS) Theory and Institutional Theory, this study develops a comprehensive socio-technical governance framework using a Design Science Research (DSR) strategy mapped across the six layers of Saunders' Research Onion. The framework establishes three core operational pillars-Responsibility Allocation, Continuous Auditability, and Dynamic Institutional Alignment-enabling organizations to maintain verifiable human accountability and mitigate system drift without requiring access to proprietary source code or trade secrets. This paper contributes an actionable governance artifact for enterprise risk leaders, auditors, and regulators seeking to align autonomous digital systems with evolving compliance mandates.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7485400\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.63108/vab.ldd.1.10\", \"title\": [\"Beyond the Black Box: A Multi Tiered Framework for Algorithmic Accountability and Liability in Autonomous Decision Making Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of making decisions with limited human intervention, questions of responsibility and accountability have become more difficult. This paper examines two major challenges created by autonomous decision-making systems: the “black box” problem, where the reasoning behind an AI decision may be difficult to understand, and the “many hands” problem, where responsibility is spread across several actors involved in the development and use of the system. The paper further uses actor mapping to identify the different participants involved in the AI lifecycle and examines why identifying these actors alone may not be enough to determine responsibility.</jats:p>\\n                  <jats:p>To address this gap, the paper proposes a Multi-Tiered Accountability Framework based on three connected levels: technical accountability, actor-based accountability and responsibility allocation. The framework considers factors such as an actor’s contribution, level of control, foreseeability of risk and ability to prevent or reduce harm. It aims to provide a clearer and fairer approach to accountability without treating AI autonomy as a reason to remove human responsibility. The paper ultimately argues that as AI becomes more autonomous, legal accountability must develop alongside technological innovation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.63108/vab.ldd.1.10\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 10, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7486080\", \"title\": [\"The Ministerial Accountability Gap Algorithmic Decision-Making and Constitutional Fit in Westminster Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Imported algorithmic accountability tools fail in Westminster jurisdictions because they target the agency, not the minister. Algorithmic impact assessments, transparency standards, and AI assurance frameworks have been developed within the administrative-state frame of the United States and the regulatory-state frame of the European Union. They are now being imported, largely unmodified, into jurisdictions operating under Westminster constitutional architecture, where the minister is the constitutional accountability node and agencies advise rather than act. The import produces a structural accountability gap. The paper makes four calibrated contributions: it analyses the gap through the Westminster doctrinal frame; it identifies cross-architecture transplantation as the proximate mechanism; it treats algorithmic systems as the immediate deployment context in which the misalignment now bites; and it proposes a redesign vocabulary, accountability by constitutional fit. The imported AIA literature identifies the wrong accountability target. The gap manifests through four co-occurring patterns: abstraction, displacement, temporal, and scale, anchored to four Westminster cases drawn from the public record (Australia's Robodebt scheme, the UK Home Office visa streaming tool, the UK Ofqual A-level grading algorithm, and the decision-support systems of New Zealand's Accident Compensation Corporation). The redesign principle carries three operational elements: a ministerial legibility requirement, procurement-stage constitutional review, and rotation-safe decommissioning. The argument is theoretical and case selection is on the dependent variable.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7486080\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "9c7e714189e7fccf6d67c0f6f0b43f10ab4cd37d0a4f91c60f6e289c5e6dcd37", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.62311/nesx/rb-69ag-978-81-68314-31-3", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7485400", "doi:10.63108/vab.ldd.1.10", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7486080"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.62311/nesx/rb-69ag-978-81-68314-31-3", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7485400", "https://doi.org/10.63108/vab.ldd.1.10", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7486080"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
